10 Movies That Were Drastically Changed After Their Initial Release

Emma StefanskyUpdated: October 18, 2026
  • Share on Facebook
  • Share on Twitter
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:02
Instaread

We’ve all heard of — and probably experienced — the Mandela Effect, convinced so completely of something in the world being one way only to find out it was a totally different way all along. What gives? Were half of us suddenly shunted into a parallel universe where things are only slightly different? Were there two versions of the Berenstain/Berenstein Bears book series this whole time and everyone else is trying to drive us crazy? Or, perhaps, are we just misremembering little details about life because that’s just how human brains work? Usually we’d say the answer is that last one — except where these movies are concerned.

No, you’re not going nuts. No, you’re not remembering something a little bit wrong. All of these movies have been slightly altered from their original versions in odd ways. It’s not unheard of for movies to be changed a little — dubbed or censored for other markets, pared down for a television release, lengthened for a special edition home video. All of these changes are pretty standard. What’s not standard is whatever is going on with the movies on this list.

Some of them have been changed at the director’s discretion. Some of them have been “improved” with newer effects or altered dialogue. Others have been re-edited for their audience’s safety, or to be a better aesthetic fit with their sequels. Still others were unfinished when they were first released and cleaned up a little later. Whatever the reason any of these movies were changed, it’s almost impossible to watch most of them today the way they were originally released.

10 Movies That Were Altered After They Were Released

No, it's not the Mandela Effect, they really are different!

Gallery Credit: Emma Stefansky

Twentieth Century-Fox

Star Wars (1977)

George Lucas’ Star Wars trilogy — especially the first film — is one of the most notorious examples of a director going a little too hard re-editing his own vision. Between painting over lots of the charmingly retro effects with computer generated imagery to replacing whole characters with CGI, Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope looks very little like it did when it was first released in theaters in 1977. One change even sparked a decades-long fight in the fan community: in the original theatrical cut, Han Solo shoots bounty hunter Greedo under the table during their confrontation in the Mos Eisley cantina, but in the 1997 special edition Lucas re-edited the scene to show Greedo shooting at Han first, and missing. Fans preferred the original scene, which showed Han’s ruthlessness and street smarts — traits that would be softened over time as he took up the cause of the Rebellion.

Warner Bros.

The Shining (1980)

There are a lot of mysteries surrounding Stanley Kubrick’s adaptation of The Shining to this day, and one of them involves a scene most of us will never see. When it first debuted in theaters, the movie had an extra epilogue scene at the very end, showing Wendy Torrance recovering in a hospital bed and talking to Danny and hotel manager Stuart Ullman. Ullman tells her that Jack’s corpse couldn’t be found on the grounds of the Overlook, and then hands Danny what appears to be the same yellow tennis ball he’s seen playing with inside the hotel. Kubrick had the scene cut from the physical prints of the film one week into its theatrical run, sending the film back to Warner Bros. where it was either destroyed or lost in some vault somewhere. For many the scene’s loss is a bit of a blessing, since it raised too many irrelevant questions right at the end of the movie.

Universal Pictures

E.T. The Extra Terrestrial (1982)

The extended 20th Anniversary Special Edition of E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial isn’t quite the same kind of lost media as the scene from The Shining, but it’s not easy to find. This version of the movie includes lots of Steven Spielberg-mandated alterations, such as CGI modifications to streamline some of the effects, altered dialogue (in one scene replacing the word “terrorist” with “hippie” due to post-9/11 sensitivity around the term), and, worst of all, editing out the guns wielded by the federal agents trying to stop Elliott and his friends on their bikes, and replacing the weapons with walkie-talkies — removing the sense of inherent danger from the scene. Spielberg later admitted that that had been a mistake, and has said that future versions of the movie should stay true to the original cut.

Warner Bros.

The Matrix (1999)

If you’ve ever seen all of the Matrix movie posters lined up together, you’ll notice something strange: all of the sequels have a distinct green tinge, while the first movie appears mostly blue and gray. Hasn’t The Matrix always been green? Well, not exactly. In The Matrix Reloaded and The Matrix Revolutions, the Wachowskis and their director of photography Bill Pope decided to add a green hue to all of the scenes that took place inside the Matrix to evoke a sense of unreality. They didn’t have that idea in time for the first movie, though, so the original theatrical release of The Matrix was mostly the blue-gray we all remember, even the scenes inside the program. It wasn’t until the movie was re-released in 2008 that it took on that sickly green hue, confusing longtime fans who may have started to believe we were living in a simulation.

Buena Vista Pictures Distribution

Lilo & Stitch (2002)

We can’t give the children too many bad ideas! In the original release of Lilo & Stitch in most countries, during an early scene where Nani is chasing Lilo around their house, Lilo hides inside of a clothes dryer, shutting the door to keep Nani from finding her. (It doesn’t work; Nani knows her tricks.) For the UK release of the film, in order to secure a U (Universal) rating, the scene was edited to show Lilo climbing inside a cupboard and using a pizza box as the “door” so as not to give children any bad ideas about trapping themselves inside dryer machines. That edit has now become the official version since the movie was added to Disney+ and for all subsequent home releases. (That scene was far from the biggest change though: Have you ever seen the airplane sequence that was completely re-animated after 9/11?)

Universal Pictures

Bruce Almighty (2003)

Ever try to call God on your phone? After Bruce Almighty came out in theaters, a lot of people did — enough that the movie had to be altered because of it. During the scene where God is calling Bruce on his cell phone — no matter how hard he tries to destroy it — an actual phone number (776-2323) shows up on the screen. The producers had made sure that the number was not actually in use in Bruce’s area code, but didn’t check anywhere else in the country, which led to an epidemic of random people and businesses receiving incessant phone calls from fans who wanted to see if God would answer. (One of the “victims” was a church in North Carolina whose minister, coincidentally, was named Bruce.) To put a stop to the madness, the number was changed to 555-0123 for the movie’s release on home video and television.

Walt Disney Studios Motion PIctures

Incredibles 2 (2018)

Screenslaver, the main villain in Disney’s Incredibles 2, takes control of their victims by hacking into any nearby screen and bombarding them with hypnotically flashing lights. When the film came out in theaters, many people found themselves affected by the lights, and disability advocates noted that they were aggressive enough to cause epileptic seizures in people prone to them. Some theaters and eventually Disney themselves posted warnings about the lights before screenings, and for the film’s release in the U.K. the scene where Elastigirl fights Screenslaver was re-edited so that the flashing passes the Harding test, which tests flashing sequences for photosensitive epilepsy.

Sony Pictures Releasing

Venom (2018)

Venom, the movie where Tom Hardy plays a journalist whose body becomes enmeshed with an alien symbiote, was never meant to be taken wholly seriously. The concept is silly, the execution leaves a lot to be desired, and Venom himself is pretty goofy by design. That said, the movie leans a little too far into the goofiness at certain points — notably during a fight scene where a SWAT soldier lets out a loud “Wilhelm scream” after Venom throws him off a balcony. The stock sound effect, which originated in the 1951 film Distant Drums, has become something of an inside joke in Hollywood, but the sheer obviousness of it in Venom caused more than a few complaints. The scream was subsequently removed from all Blu-ray releases of the film.

Universal Pictures

Cats (2019)

Yes, by now we’ve probably all heard of the proverbial “butthole cut” of Tom Hooper’s musical atrocity Cats, but the pervasiveness of that particular story glossed over the fact that most of the animation in the movie was still pretty bad when it was released in theaters. The movie features extensive digital effects that convert actors in motion capture suits into half-cat-half-humanoid beasts — which were finished mere hours before the official premiere. Well, mostly finished. During the first week of its wide release, audiences noticed weird CGI glitches like Judi Dench’s human hand and wedding ring appearing instead of her cat paw, and body parts of other characters clipping though their fur. Days later, Universal advised all theaters to replace the original version of the movie with an updated one featuring cleaned up VFX.

Sony Pictures Releasing

Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse (2023)

It’s no secret that the production of the Spider-Verse movies is nothing short of a years-long extremely arduous digital marathon. But, no matter how much time filmmakers have to iron out the kinks, things can still go wrong. When Sony’s animated Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse swung into theaters, some fans were perplexed by the odd, often off, sound-mixing in the movie, particularly during the opening scene where it was almost impossible to hear Gwen Stacy’s introductory narration over the soundtrack. Even though only some showings were affected, it was bad enough that the studio sent out a new version to all theaters with improved sound balances. But the problems didn’t stop there: It appeared, for a while, that there were two slightly different versions of the movie playing at the same time with minor changes that made some viewers feel like perhaps they’d slipped into an alternate Spider-Verse of their own.

10 Famous Movies That Sparked Completely Bizarre Lawsuits

These movies were taken to court for reasons you'd never predict.

Gallery Credit: Emma Stefansky

Paramount Pictures

The Elephant Man (1980)

David Lynch’s The Elephant Man, a biopic about Joseph Merrick, a man with significant physical deformities who nonetheless was an accomplished artist and member of society in the late 1800s, seems like another of Lynch’s one-in-a-million movie plots. But, oops, it turned out that there was a stage play with the same title and about the same subject that opened only a few years before production on Lynch’s film was set to begin. The producers of the play ended up suing the film production before filming began, and though they allowed the film to be made, The Elephant Man had to pay the play an undisclosed amount of money, and ads for the movie had to have a disclaimer telling audiences that the movie was not based on or affiliated with the play in any way.

Universal Pictures

Back to the Future Part II (1989)

Crispin Glover played the nerdy loser George McFly who grows up to be Marty McFly’s meek father in the first Back to the Future movie, a role that turned out to be his breakout in Hollywood. However, when his concerns with the shallow message of the film’s ending and request for more money to return for the sequels went ignored by director Robert Zemeckis and Universal, Glover left the franchise. Jeffrey Weissman took over the role of George for Part II, wearing facial prosthetics to blend in with reused footage of Glover from the previous movie. Glover sued, claiming the film had copied his likeness without permission and hadn’t compensated him for the footage, and was awarded money in a settlement out of court.

Universal Pictures

Reality Bites (1994)

Screenwriter Helen Childress has been open about how her script for Reality Bites, the rom-com-dram about four college graduates navigating the chaos of the 1990s economic recession, was inspired by real events and real people from her own life. This factoid, otherwise a mildly interesting detail about the origins of the movie, would come back to, well, bite. Film financier Troy Diller, who shares a name with Ethan Hawke’s character in the movie, sued Childress, director Ben Stiller, and producer Danny DeVito, claiming his life had been upended by inquiries from friends and potential clients who assumed that, because the movie was based loosely on real people, the real Troy Diller had done and said the same things the fictional one had. Dyer and the filmmakers settled the suit when Childress sent him a written confirmation that the film was not in fact based on him.

20th Century Fox

Jingle All the Way (1996)

People claim that successful movies stole their ideas all the time, but this one was nearly legit. Jingle All the Way, the Christmas comedy about two dads fighting over an action figure for their respective kids, was itself the subject of a dispute when a publishing company that had bought a similar screenplay written by a high school teacher sued 20th Century Fox claiming that they’d stolen the idea. Basically, the publisher claimed they’d sent the script to a number of studios including Fox, but all of them had rejected it, only for a movie to come out a few years later with the same basic premise, same character names, and same or similar lines of dialogue.

At first, Fox was found liable for copyright infringement, but after some back and forth and an appeal from Fox, a judge noted that the production company had bought the Jingle All the Way script well before they’d had an opportunity to read the other one, so it was impossible for them to have copied it.

Warner Bros.

The Devil's Advocate (1997)

Legal drama The Devil’s Advocate was embroiled in some real-life legal drama when an artist claimed his work had been copied for the movie without his knowledge or consent. In the film, the devilish John Milton has a striking sculpture in his office featuring lots of organic wind/water formations and bas-reliefs of people floating around within. At first glance, it’s very similar to an actual sculpture designed by Frederick Hart that was installed above the doors of the Washington National Cathedral — a fact that didn’t go unnoticed by Hart himself, who sued Warner Bros. for copyright infringement.

Warner Bros. claimed they had no knowledge of his artwork and so couldn’t have copied it on purpose. When a judge ruled that the home video release of the film would be delayed unless the two sides could reach an agreement, Warner Bros. decided to edit the scene for future releases and put stickers on the tapes that already existed affirming that there was no relation between the movie and Hart’s artwork.

20th Century Fox

Borat (2006)

Sacha Baron Cohen’s Borat was purposefully designed to ruffle as many feathers as possible, and a lot of those feathers made their way into the American courts. Two frat bros featured in the film sued for defamation, a Macedonian Romani singer claimed the film used her song without permission, a driving instructor claimed the producers had lied about the content of the film and said he’d never have agreed to participate if he’d known what it really was. Probably the most famous of these suits is the one raised by a Romanian village, whose residents claimed they were lied to, defamed, and paid paltry amounts of money to compensate them for their involvement. The case was dismissed both times it was filed in court, and 20th Century Fox claimed Baron Cohen had done his part for the village, donating money, computers, and school supplies.

20th Century Fox

Avatar (2009)

James Cameron’s space opera Avatar was the culmination of pretty much everything he had ever been interested in putting on film, from beautiful aliens to giant robots to otherworldly vistas on far-off planets. Those vistas caught the eye of Roger Dean, the fantasy artist and album cover designer for bands like Yes and Asia, who saw more than a few similarities to his own work in the movie’s landscape shots of Pandora’s floating islands and arc-shaped rock formations. Dean attempted to sue Cameron for using his work as inspiration without credit, citing 14 of his paintings as evidence of copyright infringement. The judge ultimately dismissed the suit, saying that while the film and Dean’s artwork share similarities, Dean himself doesn’t have a “monopoly” on any of the concepts present in his imagery.

Warner Bros.

The Hangover Part II (2011)

Many of these lawsuits expose odd, thorny legal issues that are difficult to completely decide on one way or another, and the lawsuit leveled against The Hangover Part II is one of these. In the film, Ed Helms’ character wakes up along with his amnesiac comrades with Mike Tyson’s famous tattoo etched into his face and no memory of how it got there. When the film was released, the tattoo artist who originally inked the design onto Tyson filed a lawsuit alleging that the film had stolen his copyrighted material. Warner Bros. argued that tattoos weren’t copyrightable but a judge agreed they were, allowing the suit to go to court. Ultimately, Warner Bros. and the artist settled for an undisclosed sum.

Neon

Colossal (2016)

Nacho Vigalondo’s sci-fi drama Colossal stars Anne Hathaway as a depressed woman whose self-destructive habits manifest as a literal giant kaiju monster that terrorizes Seoul. But the film’s legal troubles began before production had even started. After production company Voltage Pictures released the movie’s logline mentioning a woman with a psychic connection to a giant monster that flattens an Asian city, Toho, the Japanese company that owns Godzilla, sued to ensure that the monster in the movie wouldn’t stray too close to Godzilla’s design. Toho and Voltage eventually settled, and Vigalondo and Voltage agreed not to copy any aspects of Godzilla’s look or behavior in designing their creature.

Universal Pictures

Yesterday (2019)

Stan armies are no joke. Just a few years ago, the fans of one actress even attempted to take a studio to court. A trailer for Yesterday, the Danny Boyle movie where the Beatles suddenly disappear from the world and everyone except for one man forgets they existed, features Ana de Armas prominently —t he actress was originally cast to play a secondary love interest. But when two de Armas fans paid to rent the movie on Amazon Prime, only to discover all of her scenes were cut after test screenings, they attempted to sue Universal Pictures.

Their suit accused Universal of false advertising; Universal countered with the argument that trailers were works of art and protected under the First Amendment. Ultimately, everyone settled, and no one had to pay anyone anything — though the two fans were liable for some pretty hefty attorney’s fees.
Source: 10 Movies That Were Drastically Changed After Their Initial Release
